clue.text: Trust managed church without priest

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: managed means ran, as in ran a business
Eli is the priest in the Old Testament who raised Samuel
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A trust is run by a church that has no priest of its own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking. Eli is the crossword's stock priest.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: placing reliance in someone is placing trust in them.

clue.text: Nice way to retain line in exhortation to Britannia

indicators.note: to retain means to keep something held inside

parts.note: in Nice, a French city, a street or way is a rue

explanation.surface: A French street somehow keeps a line from a patriotic British song.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice is the French city, not the adjective, which is why the way is French. 'Rule, Britannia!' is the patriotic song sung at the Last Night of the Proms.
explanation.definitionFit: The first word of the song title 'Rule, Britannia!' is an exhortation addressed to Britannia.

clue.text: Composer picked up record

indicators.note: picked up as in heard, so the clue gives a word that sounds like another

parts.note: Franz Liszt, the Hungarian composer and pianist

explanation.surface: A composer collected a recording.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: to list items is to record them, and a list is a written record.

clue.text: At the intervals matrons ogled composer

indicators.note: at the intervals means taking letters at regular gaps, here every second one

explanation.surface: During concert intervals, matronly ladies eyed up a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'intervals' suggests concert breaks, but here it picks the even letters of 'matrons ogled'.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Malcolm Arnold was an English composer of symphonies and film scores.

clue.text: Come to our gigs dressed up — it's René's big idea

indicators.note: dressed up suggests the letters are rearranged in a new outfit

explanation.surface: An invitation to come to gigs in finery, joined to a remark about a philosopher's notion.
explanation.walkthrough: René is René Descartes, whose famous Latin conclusion means 'I think, therefore I am'.
explanation.definitionFit: Descartes' best-known philosophical principle is this Latin phrase, his foundational idea.

clue.text: Solo contribution from Ontario soprano

indicators.note: contribution from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A singer from Canada provides a solo piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An arioso is a melodic vocal passage for a single voice, between recitative and aria.

clue.text: Musical's opening snubbed for 12

indicators.note: snubbed means cut off, so the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: Brigadoon is a Lerner and Loewe stage musical about a Scottish village

explanation.surface: The start of a stage show is snubbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 points to the answer at 12-across, OLD-TIME DANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the rigadoon is a lively Baroque dance of French origin, so an old-time dance.

clue.text: Pipe controls medical emergency?

definitions.meaning: the knobs on a pipe organ that bring ranks of pipes in or out
read as a phrase, a body organ that has stopped working

explanation.surface: Controls on pipes cause a medical crisis.
explanation.definitionFit: Organ stops govern which pipes sound; read literally, an organ stopping is a medical emergency.

clue.text: See 9
Gosh, isn't the platform busy tonight!

definitions.text: Gosh, isn't the platform busy tonight!

indicators.note: busy suggests bustle and activity, so the letters before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at how crowded the stage is this evening.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the anagram and a fair description: the stage at the Royal Albert Hall is packed on that night.
explanation.definitionFit: The final concert of the BBC Proms season is famously crowded and exuberant, so the exclamation fits that evening.

clue.text: Daily, one with good character, figures on staff

parts.note: The Times is a daily newspaper
I is the Roman numeral for one
nature means character or disposition

explanation.surface: A newspaper and a person of good character work out numbers for employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like employees but is the musical stave of five lines.
explanation.definitionFit: The pair of numbers at the start of a stave of music, such as 3/4, give the metre.

clue.text: For joint performance both undressed

parts.note: a gig is a live music performance

indicators.note: undressed means stripped of the outer covering, so the outside letters go

explanation.surface: Two performers appear naked in a joint show.
explanation.definitionFit: A gigot is a leg of lamb or mutton, a cut of meat, so a joint.

clue.text: Perhaps saunter on at middle C, modulating to E

indicators.note: modulating means changing key, so here the letters change their order

explanation.surface: A piece of music shifts from middle C into the key of E.
explanation.walkthrough: The saunter is a ballroom sequence dance, so 'Perhaps' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the saunter is a slow sequence dance of the kind danced in old-fashioned ballrooms.

clue.text: A short way to a new school turns up in old document

indicators.note: turns up in a down clue means the whole is read from bottom to top
short means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: a track is a path or way
a gam is a school of whales

explanation.surface: A shortcut to a new school is found in an old document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims TRACK to TRAC, and 'turns up' reverses the whole chain ATRACANGAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the charter of rights sealed by King John in 1215 is a historic document.

clue.text: College shows signs of decay? Times probes funds

indicators.note: probes means pushes into, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: uni is short for university, a college
rusts are the visible signs of metal corroding
T is the abbreviation for time, so times plural gives two of them

explanation.surface: A college looks run down, and a newspaper investigates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper but is the plural of T, the time abbreviation, giving TT.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: these are collective investment schemes pooling savers' money, a kind of fund.

clue.text: GW Russell holds service for composer

indicators.note: holds means contains, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: George William Russell, the Irish poet, wrote under the pen name AE
RN is the Royal Navy, one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A writer is said to include a church service for a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Arne wrote 'Rule, Britannia!', sung at the Last Night of the Proms.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Thomas Arne was an eighteenth-century English composer.

clue.text: Blowpipe exercises with a small horn

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercises
a hooter is a car horn

explanation.surface: A blowpipe plays exercises alongside a little horn, as if in a band.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: a tube for blowing dried peas at targets is a simple blowpipe.

clue.text: Like Fingal's Cave in paper format

definitions.meaning: Fingal's Cave on Staffa in Scotland is made of hexagonal basalt pillars
set out in vertical blocks of text, as a newspaper prints its articles

explanation.surface: A famous sea cave is described as being in newspaper form.
explanation.walkthrough: Mendelssohn's overture The Hebrides is also called Fingal's Cave, a Proms favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: The cave's walls are built of pillar-shaped rock, and newspaper text is laid out in vertical columns.

clue.text: No time to record an attempt to cover number recently

indicators.note: to cover means to go round, so one piece contains another

parts.note: a log is a record, as in a ship's log
an is the indefinite article, A
a go is an attempt

explanation.surface: No time to record a try at covering a song.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a phrase meaning only a short while back, synonymous with lately.

clue.text: Musical faux pas by Mike

indicators.note: faux is French for false, so the short word after it is given in a false order

parts.note: M is Mike in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A singer commits a blunder alongside someone called Mike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faux pas' reads as one blunder, but 'faux' is the anagram signal working on 'pas'. The definition is loose: the Monty Python stage show built on the Spam sketch is Spamalot.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusion: the Monty Python sketch about the tinned meat ends in a Viking chorus and became the stage musical Spamalot.

clue.text: Woman stealing Catholic writer's plot

indicators.note: stealing means taking something in, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: she refers to a woman
the writer refers to themself as me, and writer's means writer is

explanation.surface: A woman steals a Catholic author's storyline.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: a plot or plan is a scheme, especially a secret one.

clue.text: Sorceress's inner sanctum's poor condition

indicators.note: inner says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Circe is the sorceress of Greek myth who turned Odysseus's men into pigs

indicators.note: poor suggests a bad state, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the word sanctum, a private retreat, taken as written for the jumble

explanation.surface: A witch's private chamber is in a bad state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' jumbles the letters into UMSTANC before 'inner' places them. Pomp and Circumstance is the Elgar march sung at the Last Night of the Proms.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: one's circumstance is one's condition or situation.

clue.text: Brief report describes prom's final ceremony

indicators.note: describes in its old sense of draws round, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: a pop is a short sharp sound, a brief report like a gun's

indicators.note: final means only the last letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A short account describes the end of a Prom concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describes' means draws a line round; 'report' is a bang, not an account.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: pomp is grand ceremonial display.

clue.text: Scots know about royal composer

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: ken is the Scots word for know
R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN

explanation.surface: The Scots are aware of a composer to the monarchy.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Jerome Kern was the American composer of Show Boat.

clue.text: Is this playing in Rossini composition for strings?

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters perform in a new arrangement together

explanation.surface: A question about whether something is played in an opera composer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this' stands for the answer: IS plus the answer, rearranged, spells ROSSINI.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosin is the resin rubbed on bows so that they grip violin and cello strings.

clue.text: Spy cases hotel on river in Cornish port

indicators.note: cases means encloses, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: a mole is a spy planted inside an organisation

indicators.note: on means placed after in an across answer

parts.note: the Ouse is a river in England
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A spy checks out a riverside hotel in a Cornish town.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Mousehole is a fishing village and harbour in Cornwall, the county at England's south-west tip.

clue.text: R Strauss bad? Silly not using stars, ludicrous!

indicators.note: silly suggests the letters are messed about
not using says certain letters of the fodder are left out of the rearrangement

explanation.surface: A critic calls Richard Strauss bad and silly for not using star performers.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of 'R Strauss bad', drop those of 'stars', and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: absurd and ludicrous both mean ridiculously unreasonable.

clue.text: Safe to slate young piper in play

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
to slate and to pan both mean to criticise harshly

explanation.surface: A safe is used to criticise a young musician in a theatre production.
explanation.walkthrough: J M Barrie's boy who never grows up plays pan pipes.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Barrie's play features a boy who never grows up and plays the pipes.
